summary: This is a humorous April 1st RFC. It parodies RFC 2119, which defines key words like MUST and SHOULD, by inventing extra requirement words for situations the originals cannot capture. It is a joke, not a real specification.

eli5.summary: This is a joke rulebook. It makes up silly new ways to say "you have to do this," like a game where the rules are the punchline.

questions: must but we know you won't meaning
subtitle: An April 1st spoof that adds nine hedging phrases to the RFC 2119 requirement words.

tldr.problem: RFC 2119 gives authors a standard set of requirement words, but this joke says many documents find they cannot capture the nuance of real specifications.
tldr.mechanism: It defines nine tongue-in-cheek phrases, from MUST (BUT WE KNOW YOU WON'T) to MIGHT, each with a wry definition and a real quotation from an older RFC.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental, Independent Submission published on 1 April 2013 and is not a real requirements vocabulary.

today: RFC 6919 is an April 1st Experimental document that the RFC Editor published independently of any other RFC stream. It is not obsoleted or updated, but it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard. The real requirement words remain those of RFC 2119.

sections.title: An April 1st Parody of RFC 2119
sections.content:
RFC 6919 is an April 1st joke document. It plays on RFC 2119, the document that defines words such as MUST and SHOULD for describing the requirements of a specification. The joke is that many IETF documents find those words cannot accurately capture the nuanced requirements of their specification.

Authors who 'follow these guidelines' are told to add a boilerplate sentence listing nine new key words: "MUST (BUT WE KNOW YOU WON'T)", "SHOULD CONSIDER", "REALLY SHOULD NOT", "OUGHT TO", "WOULD PROBABLY", "MAY WISH TO", "COULD", "POSSIBLE" and "MIGHT".
sections.eli5: Grown-ups who write rules use words like 'must' and 'should.' This memo jokes that they need sillier words, like 'might,' for when nobody is really sure.

sections.title: The Strong and Cautious Phrases
sections.content:
MUST (BUT WE KNOW YOU WON'T) marks requirements needed to meet formal review criteria, such as mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms, when implementers find them too inconvenient to implement. If the parenthetical is present, authors MUST give a reason in it. The example rewrites a sentence from RFC 6120 about SCRAM, adding that implementers will not comply because their TLS library does not support extracting channel binding information.

SHOULD CONSIDER means the authors think implementations should do something but are not sure quite what. REALLY SHOULD NOT flags dangerous behavior that some important vendor still does, so the authors could not make it MUST NOT. OUGHT TO is an optimistic assertion of behavior that is clearly morally right and needs no substantiation.
sections.eli5: Some of the new words mean 'you have to, but we know you will not,' or 'you should do something, but we are not sure what.' It is like a teacher saying 'please try,' when they know you will not.

sections.title: The Hedging Phrases
sections.content:
WOULD PROBABLY states the authors' expectation of what a reasonable implementation is likely to do. The RFC adds that there is no requirement for implementations to be reasonable, and calls the phrase an example of the 'passive-aggressive voice'.

MAY WISH TO marks a behavior that seems appealing to some and ridiculous or unnecessary to others, often used to avoid further delay in approval. COULD gives a hint that might be critical to reliable or secure operation without a hard requirement, which allows vendor product differentiation. POSSIBLE describes what some working group members thought of as an edge case that will never happen but that in practice lets the protocol work at the most fundamental level. MIGHT conveys a requirement in an intentionally stealthy fashion, to facilitate product differentiation.

Each phrase comes with a real quotation from an earlier RFC, such as RFC 3501, RFC 5888 or RFC 6733, to show the style in use.
sections.eli5: The rest are polite maybes. 'Could' and 'might' sound like a gentle suggestion, but they let companies do their own thing and still say they followed the rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The joke closes with a straight-faced security section. It says IETF documents have traditionally expressed security requirements with a mixture of RFC 2119 words and the phrases above. The RFC 2119 words are principally useful when threats and mitigations are clear and well defined. The new key words can be applied when the threat model is ambiguous, and mitigations are unclear or inconvenient.
sections.eli5: When nobody knows exactly what could go wrong, these made-up words let writers sound serious without promising anything.
